speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Specifically, the Bill introduces three key areas of amendments to the FTZ Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Before I go into the specifics of each amendment, let me explain why we are making these changes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: We have thrived economically as a nation by situating ourselves as a trading hub and crucial node in global supply chains.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Today, Singapore is the second busiest container port in the world and the largest transshipment hub, handling about a fifth of the world's container transshipment traffic.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: In 2022, our port handled a container throughput of over 37 million 20-foot equivalent units (TEUs), mostly for transshipment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Our airport handled another two million tonnes of air cargo, a significant proportion of which is also transshipment cargo.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Our geographical location and connectivity give us a natural advantage as a trading hub.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: But what helps to further strengthen our attractiveness as a hub is our FTZs which facilitate transshipment activities and support more efficient and resilient global supply chains through a hub-and-spoke model.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: There are, currently, 10 FTZs in Singapore, located mainly at our sea and air terminals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Businesses that operate within the FTZs enjoy exemption from customs duties and taxes on re-exports, simplified customs procedures, access to streamlined logistics and transportation services, as well as other services to facilitate their trade operations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: These are pro-business elements we want to preserve when we amend the legislation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: There has been growing concerns of FTZs around the world being misused for illicit activities, such as weapons proliferation, environmental crimes and trade-based money laundering.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Illegal actors will try to disguise their actions as legitimate trade, for example, by falsely declaring cargo manifest data, or by swapping out legitimate goods with contraband before re-exporting.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Singapore Customs has been taking proactive measures to combat and deter illicit activities within our FTZs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: For instance, Customs regularly conducts surprise inspections on businesses operating within the FTZs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Enforcement actions are taken against those found to be engaging in illicit trade.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: To better target suspicious firms, Customs also works closely with our FTZ authorities, as well as local and international partners, to share actionable intelligence and operational support to strengthen our ability to detect illicit activities and enforce against illegal actors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: The aim of the legislative amendments is to update and strengthen our FTZ regime to keep pace with evolving threats and the increasing sophistication of illegal actors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: We are proposing changes in this Bill to further enhance the regulation and control of goods that flow through our FTZs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: In the past, our FTZs were operated by public bodies that were appointed by the Minister for Finance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Through the licensing regime, we will be able to specify and enforce the necessary requirements to ensure the overall security of our FTZs and improve our regulation of the flow of goods and persons within the FTZ.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: For example, FTZ operators will be required to put in place necessary security structures like CCTVs and fences and provide assistance to officers of customs in the performance of their official duties.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Our FTZ authorities have already put many of these measures in place today and the proposed amendments will formalise these requirements in legislation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: FTZ operators will also need to screen persons who intend to operate in the FTZ and manage the sub-leasing of premises in the FTZ.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: They will also need to report and disclose relevant information on suspicious or dangerous goods or persons within the FTZs to the DG of Customs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: The second key amendment of the Bill seeks to regulate the cargo handlers and cargo agents operating within the FTZ.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: While cargo handlers and agents will not be subject to a licensing regime, the proposed amendments seek to clearly lay out their responsibilities in terms of securing the goods under their charge and data provision.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Specifically, cargo handlers will be responsible for monitoring and managing the movement of goods handled at their premises within the FTZs and ensuring their premises are secure.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: They will need to report goods that may have contravened our laws.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Cargo handlers and cargo agents will also need to provide specified information contained in a bill of lading or airway bill in advance of their entry or transshipment of their goods through Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Currently, only information relating to goods that are imported, exported or controlled goods that are transshipped, is required to be submitted as part of the permit application process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: With this amendment, information on all transshipment goods will need to be submitted.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: These amendments will give us better visibility of goods that are being transshipped through Singapore before arriving at their final destination.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Customs can monitor the flows of goods for signs of illicit activity and take the necessary action, in close partnership with other international authorities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: The third set of amendments sets out the enforcement powers of the DG and officers of Customs and the regulatory actions they may undertake.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: The proposed amendments in this Bill have been carefully calibrated, in consultation with industry and relevant stakeholders, to improve Customs' ability to detect illicit activities, while keeping our regime efficient and pro-business for companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: They are also in line with international best practices, including those established by the World Customs Organization.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Our connectivity brings goods and people through Singapore, strengthens global supply chains, boosts our economy and creates good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: As the busiest transshipment hub in the world, a significant amount of cargo comes through us daily.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: The vast majority is legitimate, but there will be a small minority who seek to flout the rules.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: We will facilitate trade, but we do not want to be misused by bad actors for their illegal means.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: The amendments in this Bill are targeted at these players, while keeping a business-friendly operating environment for genuine users.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Companies that do legitimate trade through Singapore will benefit from a sound, reputable and pro-business regime.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: In turn, Singapore continues to remain competitive as the top port-of-call for transshipments and a trusted global trading hub.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They are governed by the Free Trade Zones Act 1966, which we enacted shortly after our Independence in order to facilitate the entrepot trade which we had become known for.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Since Singapore's early days as a British colony, its geographical location at the centre of major trade routes attracted traders to ship their goods here with the aim of re-exporting them elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I note that the FTZs Act has not been substantially amended many times since it was first enacted in 1966.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I note the Senior Minister of State's speech highlighting that it is meant to update and strengthen the FTZ regime.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But could the Senior Minister of State provide further details as to why it was not done much earlier?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Is this amendment more of form than substance, or is it the case that, with this change, the Ministry will look to license other FTZ operators?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is also unclear if this seemingly unnecessary change will bring about an increase in regulatory or compliance costs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, will the existing operators have to pay more to apply for and maintain their licence as FTZ operators?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My concern is that they could seek to pass these cost increases on to the businesses and companies which operate in the FTZs, which may erode the more business-friendly conditions within these FTZs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: More importantly, how do our FTZs measure up in terms of competitiveness against the "free zones" operated by other major trading countries, especially those in the region?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Based on a study by the World Customs Organization, it appears to be getting harder to differentiate between the regulation and operation of the "free zones" in various countries.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What can we do to maintain our advantage as the transshipment hub of choice for traders and shippers?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While I understand that the form and manner of such reporting are to be prescribed in subsidiary legislation, will we be adopting the harmonised digital solutions and data standards which the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) has been working with other foreign ports to develop?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Have any exercises been undertaken to consult the current industry practice on such data submissions and have they been completed?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When will these reporting obligations be expected to come into force?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, a customs officer may enter an FTZ to monitor compliance with the Act, search the FTZ, detain goods for inspection, require persons to provide information and documents, just to name a few.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Does this mean that the customs officers did not have these powers before this?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How then have we ensured that our FTZs are free of money laundering, terrorist financing or any other illicit activities over the years?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These changes are also, according to the Ministry's public consultation documents, meant to enable better "detection, deterrence and prevention of money laundering" and associated terrorist financing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To this end, these objectives to improve efficiency as well as safety are sound and should be supported.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My comments will briefly touch on some aspects of the Bill before moving on to discuss broader considerations about how FTZs operate in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will then try to close with reflections on the evolving nature of FTZs in our global economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This vests significant discretionary power to the DG and there is some ambiguity and uncertainty in terms of its scope and application.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What conditions does the Ministry expect such prohibitions to be exercised?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One could imagine cases where a fugitive or would-be fugitive seeks refuge in the zone, in which case, certainly, national laws and regulations would naturally apply.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Would the Ministry consider requiring the DG to publish the underlying rationale for any prohibitions imposed when exercised?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: By doing so, the DG can provide greater transparency on when it uses its discretionary powers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is reasonable, but the process of submitting such reports appears to place the onus on the agents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There does not appear to be any routine reporting, for instance, unless specifically asked to do so by the DG.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This provides incentive for operators and handlers that hope to avoid taking on additional regulatory burdens to remain somewhat conservative in their assessment of when goods may justify reporting.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As far as I can gather, the Bill does not provide guidance on, say, red flags or other thresholds associated with potentially suspicious goods.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It may be, therefore, useful to include in a Schedule, in an annex, for instance, predetermined frameworks on what the Ministry believes to be appropriate thresholds or red flags.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: A sufficiently clear and comprehensive set of guidelines will allow operators to continue applying flexibility in determining what falls within or without the threshold, but ensure that all appropriate cases are flagged for possible investigation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such an action also removes the possibility of excess discretion that the Ministry might not wish to confer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While I appreciate that such snap suspensions can serve a purpose when seeking to arrest illegal or illicit activity without triggering suspicion, such actions could have detrimental effects on regular business operations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I have had residents meet with me, to be fair, in other contexts, where their operational licences were suspended with relatively limited buffer for them to rectify violations, or even while good faith negotiations over addressing highlighted problems appeared to be ongoing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Will the Ministry confirm that, as a matter of course, the FTZ operators will be offered a brief but essential window of opportunity for compliance to written notices under section 14P(3)?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For instance, the DG can specify the time for a notice under section 14P(6) to take effect, say, 14 days after the date of service of notice on the licensee, which would be consistent with section 14P(3)(c).

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Of course, this will only apply to section 14P1(a) through (c), since national security should supersede business disruptions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Nevertheless, this modification, I believe, would provide some grace period for otherwise legitimate business operations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: More generally, apart from the DG having the legal power to take measures or engage in necessary actions to ensure compliance by operators, it remains unclear how such compliance may be ascertained.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Similarly, at the licensee level, the systems and procedures that licensees are required to implement to monitor the security and movement of goods within the FTZ are also not spelt out.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But it remains to be asked how will the Bill truly advance this goal?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, the proof of the pudding is in the eating and, as we have seen in recent times, in the context of real estate, for instance, a surfeit of laws will remain ineffectual so long as compliance is insufficiently observed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even in the context of free zones, multiple reports have swirled around alleged illicit activities within "Le Freeport", which raises questions of how rigorous the process of due diligence and compliance with regulation truly is.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Some of these activities have included tax evasion, storage of looted goods, besides money laundering and terrorist financing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One is left to wonder then how the Ministry believes that this devolution to licensed FTZ operators and cargo handlers will improve the practice of due diligence as well as regulatory compliance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: How many FTZ operators and agents operate within our FTZs and, if this is a large number, will this dilute the quality of monitoring and reporting since small operators, in particular, can hardly be expected to sustain the sort of compliance regime that larger ones are able to muster?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In principle, traditional FTZs offer a host of benefits.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: By exempting tariffs, they facilitate the unfettered flow of goods and services which are especially critical for transshipment activities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: They also attract cross-border finance, since many typically offer an initial tax holiday, which can embed technological know-how and encourage the development of an otherwise infant industry.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And their concentration of industries in one region often promotes the exchange of information and ideas which can promote economies of both scale and scope.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Historically, our economic model has relied on entrepôt trade and foreign direct investment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And so, we have benefited as a country significantly from the presence of FTZs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is all well and good, but it is important for us to understand how the economic landscape is also shifting beneath us.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While I do not, to be clear, share this unvarnished, pessimistic view, it is undeniably true that world merchandise trade has essentially gone sideways since the mid-2000s and may have even declined as a share of output in some cases.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Staking our future on the trend of continued international integration strikes me as risky at best, and foolhardy at worst.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In any case, modern Singapore, as a major global wealth centre, is now seldom starved of investment financing, making the benefits of tax-free FTZs somewhat less compelling.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This, essentially, leaves the main advantage of FTZs, going forward, as being that of enhancing the benefits of agglomeration.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But the exchange of knowledge and information occurs largely digitally these days and, even if we continue to believe in the merits of in-person exchanges, such spillovers are by no means bound by the artificial boundaries that constitute an FTZ.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, we would surely want the entire nation to be a free-trade zone for ideas as well as active inquiry.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To this end, one may wonder whether the continued focus on FTZs as key engines of the economy – while unobjectionable on its face – may be missing the bigger picture, which would require our entire nation to be open to flows of data, information, knowledge and ideas – of course, within the boundaries of the law.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Importantly, it is insufficient to cater to such flows only from the perspective of quantitative metrics – ensuring that we have, for instance, a rapid and reliable digital infrastructure, a supportive environment for technology adoption, and adequate exposure for our companies and workers to modern innovations, all of which we do well, but also from a more subtle but just as important qualitative perspective.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This means fostering and welcoming open debate over ideas, even uncomfortable ones.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This means encouraging out-of-the-box thinking and training our workforce to be adaptable and flexible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I understand that these all fall truly outside the scope of the FTZ Bill, but we should not forget the ultimate purpose of legislative efforts of this nature.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While I believe that the changes proposed in the Bill – meant to provide for safety and efficiency – remain important ones to pursue, it remains unclear how the provisions in the Bill will truly succeed in meeting them.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As a critical trading hub, it is incumbent upon us to meet the highest international standards, whilst simultaneously reduce the impediments to trade.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The amendments in this Bill are designed to fortify our FTZ regime, allowing for enhanced oversight of goods within these zones, while preserving the efficiency that characterises our trade networks.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Notwithstanding, I would like to seek a few clarifications.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What mechanisms are in place for potential revocation?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are there plans to establish more FTZs in the future?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In cases where the DG had acted ultra vires or unreasonably, will cases of appeal be reviewed by the Minister?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, the accuracy of data submission within the FTZs is of paramount importance.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Equally crucial is how this data will be safeguarded by customs authorities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Ministry of Finance (MOF) share more information about this issue?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fourth, will there be a provision allowing for appeals against penalties imposed in cases where licensing conditions are breached or where actions conflict with the Act?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Lastly, Mr Speaker, Sir, the matter of data confidentiality merits attention.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore's FTZs at our ports and airport are an important node of business and trade for the Singapore economy to thrive and prosper safely without any hindrance and threat.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore's Free Trade Agreements (FTAs), Investment Guarantee Agreements and the Double Tax Avoidance Agreements also allow for smooth trade with many countries in the world.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: In particular, this piece of legislation is of utmost importance for both small and medium enterprises (SMEs) as well as larger companies, as it is all about the ease of doing business in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: It also gives a very clear and loud message to the investor community that Singapore means business in the proper operation of its ports of entry for goods and services.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: In my speech, I would like to highlight three key items: importance of this legislation to global trade, the benefits that our businesses get from the legislative changes and, lastly, some concerns from an SME standpoint in their participation after the changes in these amendments are accepted.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: FTZs in Singapore were first established in the 1960s to facilitate trade in dutiable goods.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The FTZs Bill was last amended in Parliament in 2014.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Much has happened in the last nine years and it is timely to update this legislation, keeping in line with recent developments in global trade.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The amendment allows many administrative responsibilities to shift to licensed FTZ operators for more efficient movement of goods.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The new tenets that allow operators and cargo holders to delegate authority are reflective of current industry practices.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The amendment seeks to strike a balance, enabling both better oversight of goods flow and ensuring efficient movement of goods.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: In providing clear definition of criminal offences, it allows the DG and staff to enforce the law with increased penalties for offences.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, this amendment also allows for a smoother transmission of information and documents, while providing greater flexibility to staff.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: I also want to highlight that the staff working in FTZs play a key role in the detection, deterrence and prevention of money laundering and financial crime.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: To help the staff to better appreciate the magnitude of the risks, we will need to, on a continuous basis, develop training roadmaps and programmes which would be conducted by the private operators for the staff performing various functions in the FTZs.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: On to some concerns regarding the SME community.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: SMEs simply lack the capabilities and resources to take a more active role in enforcement and administration, which would make it difficult for them to take advantage of the new powers for FTZ licensed operators and cargo handlers.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: SMEs will also need to understand the legal powers vested in FTZ authorities and their needs-based information-gathering procedures.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: As a vibrant trading hub, much of the work being done at the FTZs is round the clock, and SMEs may not have the scale to manage their lean workforce while balancing additional training needs.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps the Senior Minister of State can elaborate on the plans in place to assist our SMEs to help implement these changes.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The revised legislation also stands to benefit many businesses.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The new amendment allows more delegation of authority by FTZ operators and cargo holders.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: This may benefit the SMEs as well as large businesses, as they can outsource certain tasks.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: There is also a very clear list of what constitutes an offence under the Free Trade Zones (Amendment) Bill – what is permitted and prohibited, the gravity of each offence and also sentencing considerations.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The legislative changes also create a safer environment for new market players, as goods passing through Singapore’s FTZs will require stringent checks done by FTZ authorities.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Also, for SMEs aiming for a global presence, the free trade principles of this amendment will safeguard their operations and increase their brand presence internationally.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: This may also push them to adopt more digital technologies faster.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: These amendments will reinforce the high standards of compliance that will not only maintain Singapore’s strong standing as a trade hub but also attract foreign investments that have confidence in our due diligence.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: FTZs have proliferated with speed in the past few decades and become an integral part of the global supply and value chains.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But the same characteristics that make FTZs attractive to legitimate businesses also attract abuse by illicit actors and there has been, for some time now, heightened concerns of FTZs being exploited for illicit trade, including weapons proliferation, as well as trade-based money laundering operations, tax evasion and terrorist financing.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Customs and the private sector have expressed the need for better Customs procedures and controls in FTZs, leading to the development of best practices, such as the Practical Guidance on Free Zones released by the World Customs Organization in 2020/2021.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: As such, the update to the FTZ Act is timely.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This is key as the multiple actors involved in operating and governing the FTZ requires clarity about responsibilities and effective coordination, including information sharing.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For instance, the requirement for advanced data submission by shipping agents to cargo handlers and, in turn, by cargo handlers and FTZ operators to Customs, will provide greater oversight of goods, persons and operations within the FTZs.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The amendments also establish the jurisdiction that the Government and Customs have to enforce controls and the penalty framework.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Lastly, better cooperation among all actors in and around the FTZ and internationally, including the provision for data sharing, will be a great help in combatting illicit activity.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, the amendments are all sound and I support them.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But I do have a few clarifications for the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: First, while there is a need to increase oversight and controls, there needs to be balance in ensuring that the controls do not create an overly onerous burden that affects the efficiency of our FTZs, which remain vital to our entrepot hub strategy.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Further, the best controls, if poorly implemented, will also affect the competitiveness of FTZs.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This is especially true, given the diversity and volume of activities in our FTZs.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is, therefore, important to take a risk-based approach and to leverage data, technology and IT integration.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I will say with conviction that FTZs will remain core to our overall trade and economic strategy, which will, for sure, change as globalisation changes – but trade is not going away.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For example, China has recently moved to open its FTZs.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: My second clarification has to do with the need for proportionate penalties and sanctions for anyone contravening the provisions of the Act.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Equally, it is important that any illicit actors caught are prosecuted to the fullest to deter others from exploiting our FTZs.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Thirdly, the root cause of poorly implemented controls and oversight is often the lack of awareness and understanding of FTZ-related risks and vulnerabilities at all levels, including on topics, such as trade-based money laundering.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: From the businesses in the FTZs to the relevant authorities and operators to financial institutions and banking regulators, this lack of understanding not only renders the zone vulnerable to illicit activity, but also impedes the ability to take a risk-based approach to management, enforcement and supervision efforts.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There is a need for a strong focus on adequate training programmes to ensure better understanding and identification of risks and an understanding of the requirements and processes under the new regime.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What are the steps being taken to step up such training?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I am sure there are other measures being looked at that did not factor in these acts.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What other preventive measures are being put in place to counter these threats?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Notwithstanding the clarifications above, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: These zones have been instrumental in the evolution of trade for the integrated supply chains of the global economy.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: According to an FIAS report, FTZs continue to benefit the country's economy.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It has been proven that it is effective in generating employment, increasing the volume and diversity of exports, serving as an essential tool for attracting foreign direct investments and enhancing commercial linkages for export.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: However, FTZs may also facilitate illegal and criminal activities, such as trade in counterfeit and pirated products.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: For centuries, governments have sought different ways to facilitate trade in their ports.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: One of the earliest was called free ports.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: These are designated areas open to commercial vessels where their cargo destined for re-export is exempt from customs duties.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Today, many FTZs are managed by private operators and regulated by Government authorities.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: A study concluded that the growth in private involvement in the FTZs has been beneficial, as privately-owned zones tend to offer better facilities and amenities and are more responsive to tenants' needs and provide a more comprehensive range of property management services.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: However, we must be cognisant that lightly regulated zones are attractive to parties engaged in illegal and criminal activities.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It is known that FTZs have facilitated trade in counterfeit and pirated products, as well as smuggling and money laundering.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: These areas have often provided bad actors with a relatively safe environment to carry out illicit activities.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: As such, governments will need to control these zones adequately, especially those operated by private entities, as they are focused on expanding zone occupancy and providing profitable services to these businesses.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: There is also a need to establish a more direct interest, enhance law enforcement oversight and increase the capacity and authority in monitoring zone operations.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: As most zones are operated via a hybrid and collaborative model between government and private parties, we need to further enhance and tighten the processes to ensure that it is strengthened against such exploitation.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: FTZ cargo handlers play a critical role in the supply chain and FTZs.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This is standard industry practice and will provide greater oversight of goods, persons and operations within the FTZ.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: I have a few questions for the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: What are the other areas that can be further improved to enhance the competitiveness of our FTZs?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Second, with the new data submission regime, what are the measures taken to ensure that the FTZ operators meet proper data management and cybersecurity requirements?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Third, given the evolving operating environment, how are the authorities updated on the latest threats?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In addition, given the collateral consequences of specific threats, what steps are taken to ensure that these threats do not enter Singapore in the first place?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our FTZs are the lifeblood of our entrepot trade.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Bill's primary goal to enhance the security, transparency and efficiency of our FTZs resonates deeply.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By striving to remain up-to-date with international best practices and increasing the level of oversight in our FTZs, this Bill reflects Singapore's unwavering commitment to trade with integrity and enhance global cooperation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Having said that, I would like to highlight four concerns.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The first is regarding the potential economic implications.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore has always been renowned for its competitive edge in global trade, with our FTZs being a testament to our strategic prowess.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The new regime also emphasises the importance of FTZ operators disseminating information on the FTZ Bill's requirements.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While essential, it demands a significant administrative apparatus.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is an operational dimension where efficiency is paramount.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There is a potential risk that businesses might grapple with not just costs, but also operational delays.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Additionally, the introduction of the advanced data submission requirement is undoubtedly poised to offer greater oversight.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But the pertinent question is: how will it impact the velocity of trade?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Efficient trade necessitates swift decisions and rapid movements.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Any delays could render our FTZs less attractive, especially when time-sensitive goods are involved.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is crucial that as we endeavour to make our trade zones more secure and compliant with international standards, we must ensure that these changes do not place an undue burden on our businesses, which could inadvertently stymie our growth.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, how do we anticipate businesses absorbing these costs?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They have loomed over international trade for quite some time.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, what are the considerations for amending the FTZ Act only now?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Thirdly, a point I would like to delve deeper into is the proposed penalty framework within the Bill.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A robust and effective regulatory system is defined not just by its preventive measures, but also by its punitive ones.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Will this penalty framework employ a structured, tiered approach, with penalties corresponding to the severity of non-compliance?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is crucial for our businesses to have a clear understanding of the repercussions, ensuring they can operate with certainty.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The clarity, fairness and consistency of this framework will be paramount in securing the trust and cooperation of businesses within the FTZs, also aiming to guide entities towards compliant behaviour.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Lastly, while the proposed revisions are a commendable step towards bolstering the security and efficiency of our FTZs, are these revisions comprehensive and robust enough to truly thwart the threats cited?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And beyond these amendments, what are other preventive measures that we, as a nation, are putting in place to counter such threats?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is not just about reactive measures, but about building a proactive shield that safeguards our trade reputation, ensuring that Singapore remains a beacon of trade integrity.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To conclude, the Free Trade Zones (Amendment) Bill stands as a testament to Singapore's approach to trade.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These queries hope to strike the right balance between safeguarding our trade zones from potential challenges and ensuring a thriving, business-friendly environment.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Indeed, as hon Members have pointed out, facilitating trade is critical to Singapore's survival as a small and open economy and our FTZs play an important role in supporting this.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is why we are making the amendments in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: They will keep our regime updated and responsive to the evolving threats, so that we remain a trusted and competitive trading hub.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Members raised questions around four themes: one, whether the proposed amendments are necessary and adequate to deal with evolving threats faced by our FTZs; two, whether the revised FTZ regime will affect business costs, lead to operational delays in cargo flows and affect our overall competitiveness; three, the accuracy of and safeguards around the data collected; and four, how FTZ operators are licensed and regulated.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: First, on the adequacy of the legislative amendments to combat and prevent illegitimate trade, as raised by Mr Shawn Huang, Mr Edward Chia, Ms Mariam Jaafar and Assoc Prof Jamus Lim.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Enhancing our FTZ regime is a constant endeavour.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Even as we enhance the regulatory regime with this Bill, we must expect criminals to find new ways to circumvent the rules.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We have to remain vigilant and continuously strengthen our regulatory framework to detect and deter illicit trade.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Customs will continue to review the adequacy of its regulations, take action to address gaps and ensure that we have a robust regime in place.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Not every enhancement to our regulatory regime requires legislative amendments.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Some can be operational in nature, for instance, improving sense-making and detection capabilities and stepping up enforcement efforts, which are what Singapore Customs has been doing over the years.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For example, Singapore Customs develops and refines risk profiles and indicators on an ongoing basis to more accurately identify suspicious goods before they enter Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Red flags are already made known to industry partners today, both through Singapore Customs' website and through direct engagements.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In recent years, Singapore Customs has also started using data analytics and artificial intelligence to improve its targeting and enforcement efforts.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In addition, Singapore Customs maintains strong partnerships with our other enforcement agencies and international counterparts and organisations, including the World Customs Organization, to share intelligence and best practices.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Such capability-building and international partnerships supplement our legislation and enforcement framework, forming a multi-pronged approach to detecting and deterring illicit activities within our FTZs.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Mr Edward Chia asked why we are amending the Act now.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Stronger levers will supplement Customs' broader efforts that I have just described, to build a trusted and competitive trade facilitation regime.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Most of the new requirements introduced in the Bill are practices currently performed by the FTZ authorities, such as ensuring the security of the FTZ and reporting any goods that contravene the law.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The proposed amendments seek to consolidate, standardise and codify these requirements under the FTZ Act, to ensure consistent implementation across FTZs and a more robust regulatory regime.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We do not expect the new data submission requirements to be disruptive to trade.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This is because the additional data that we are requesting from cargo agents are existing fields in the bill of lading and airway bill.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: They are standard information already provided today for the voyage and transport of goods.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The submission timelines under the FTZ regime are also aligned with current industry norms.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will facilitate transmission of the data collected by the cargo agents to Customs via existing systems where possible.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In proposing these amendments, we have consulted key industry stakeholders to ensure that these changes are designed and implemented in such a way to minimise the cost and compliance burden for companies, including our SMEs.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The proposed amendments will empower Singapore Customs to collect specified cargo data in advance of vessel arrival in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This will strengthen the ability of Customs to detect suspicious goods prior to their entry into Singapore and facilitate the conduct of timely interventions by our public agencies.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked how we can ensure that the data provided is accurate.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Indeed, criminals will not declare accurate data about their illegal goods.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This is where Singapore Customs’ sense-making and intelligence capabilities come into play – to detect discrepancies in the data submitted to pick out suspicious shipments and perform additional checks.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Yip and Mr Huang also asked how the data collected would be treated and managed, including cybersecurity requirements and other safeguards.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The transmission of cargo data to Singapore Customs will need to abide by the data management and cybersecurity standards set by the Government, such as those under the Cybersecurity Act.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In short, data collected cannot be disclosed without prior written consent of the related parties.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This also applies to requests by foreign law enforcement authorities.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Exceptions pertain only for specific circumstances, for example, to enable officers of Customs to investigate suspected offences, or to enable our public agencies to collect, compile and analyse such data for the purposes of national security.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The fourth and final theme relates to the proposed licensing regime for the FTZ operators, the new powers granted to the DG and officers of Customs, and the Government’s approach to enforcement.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Saktiandi asked if the powers granted to the officers of Customs are new and, if so, how Customs officers are empowered to carry out enforcement in the past.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Currently, officers of Customs carry out inspections and enforcement within our FTZs by drawing on the powers granted to them under the Customs Act (CA) and the Regulation of Imports and Exports Act (RIEA).

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The proposed amendments will help to set out and clarify powers that relate specifically to FTZs and consolidate these under the FTZ Act.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Yip and Mr Saktiandi sought clarifications about the proposed licensing regime and provisions for revocation or appeals where necessary.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: To qualify for an FTZ operator licence, the entity will need to demonstrate its ability to effectively operate an FTZ.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Singapore Customs will also take other relevant considerations into account, such as whether the entity has obtained the necessary approvals from other Government agencies, for example, from the Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore or the Maritime and Port Authority.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This is a key lever for Singapore Customs, the FTZ regulator, to ensure that licence holders meet the required standards for the proper and efficient functioning of the FTZ.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I wish to assure Mr Saktiandi that licence fees will be reasonable and will not impose a significant cost burden on the FTZ operators.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Other instances of non-compliance may attract penalties, such as fines, imprisonment, or both.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The penalty imposed will depend on the specific offence and will be tiered according to the severity of the offence.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: To Mr Yip’s question on whether there will be an avenue of appeal, the short answer is yes.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If the appellant is aggrieved by the DG’s decision, he or she may appeal to the Minister.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We recognise that there is a change in global supply chains, the reconfiguration of the global supply chains and trade flows.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: That part is obvious and that part we agree.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But what I do not fully agree with Assoc Prof Lim is that because of these changes, trade flows will no longer be important, global trade will no longer be important and, therefore, FTZs will no longer be important.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I think that is not quite in line with what we have seen, based on industry feedback, and also if we hear the speeches from the other Members in this House, including those with practical business experience, that is not what they are saying.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: They believe that FTZs continue to play an important role in supporting our position as a trade hub.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And when we look at PSA's container volumes this year compared to last year, it is not going down.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In fact, this year, our container volumes for PSA continues to grow.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: That is why we need to invest for the future.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We are putting in resources, building Tuas Port and expanding our container handling capacity.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We are building T5 at Changi Airport and getting ready to be able to handle more passengers and more cargo.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: All this is because we know that even though globalisation may affect global supply chains, the world still needs trade.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If we position ourselves as a trusted competitive trade hub, we can still capture a slice of the pie.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I also wish to clarify one example that Assoc Prof Jamus Lim mentioned in his speech – Le Freeport.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: He gave this as an example of how lack of compliance would affect its status as an FTZ.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is a high-security warehouse facility located near Changi Airport that is modelled after similar institutions in Geneva and Luxembourg.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Le Freeport Singapore offers climate-controlled storage solutions for both businesses and individuals, enabling storage of valuable assets, such as art, wine and precious metals.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Our trade facilitation regime today is highly competitive.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Maintaining our status as a trusted hub for global trade takes constant, proactive effort by our agencies, with support from our tripartite partners.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Our industry, our unions, our workers, everyone has been working very hard to contribute to this outcome.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The proposed amendments seek to enhance the regulation and control of goods that flow through our FTZs.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: They will strengthen Customs’ ability to detect and deter illegal actors from misusing our FTZs, while maintaining a business-friendly operating environment that minimises compliance cost and facilitates efficient transshipment of goods.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Just to be clear, and I am willing to stand corrected, but based on what I have checked, Le Freeport is located within a duty-free zone that is in the Changi Airport Logistics Hub.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And I believe that the Changi Airport Logistics Hub is one of the nine free trade zones that are within Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Again, I am willing to stand corrected on this.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: On the second matter, the Senior Minister of State has stated that free trade remains an important part of our future economy and he cited a number that is based on the fact that our ports have, in fact, had a record volume of flows.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This is heartening and I do not wish to convey the impression that I think that trade is unimportant.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The point that I was trying to make was, firstly, unless the Senior Minister of State wishes to correct this point, unless he challenges the fact that trade, merchandise trade, as a share of global GDP has stagnated for about 15 years, the reality is that we have reached a kind of a peak in terms of the amount of trade relative to GDP.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This does not mean that trade will not continue to grow as GDP grows.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But I think the point I was trying to make is that the future of free trade zones is not a growth industry, but rather one that is a mature industry and where we should focus on is much more on other areas, such as information flows.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I hope that clears up what is factually true and what is factually not true.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Second, this point about whether FTZs are going to be an area of growth or a mature sector, I think that is perhaps an area where we could agree to disagree.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Assoc Prof Lim may have his opinion, I would have my opinion.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We may not agree, but I respect that he has a different view.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I do not agree, Sir, with the characterisation that we no longer need FTZs or that trade is no longer going to be important to Singapore, for two reasons.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Globalisation is not going to proceed in the same way as what it has been in the past few decades.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is just that the supply chains will be configured differently.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The key for us is not whether trade is important or not important.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The key for us is, if this is going to continue, how do we then adjust our strategy and prepare ourselves to be ready to tap on this new landscape so that if the trade flows reconfigure, can Singapore still remain a key node in global supply chains?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But even more important than the hardware, we need the operating systems, we need the workers to be ready, we need the workers to be trained.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This is the part where Singapore is also able to, because of our strong tripartite partnership, build a strong, competitive ecosystem that will allow us to differentiate ourselves from the competitors.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, if you look at COVID-19, where many airports and ports were disrupted, we kept our airport and ports open.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We allowed supply chains to continue, we supported global supply chains to continue.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In fact, Singapore was used as a catch-up port by many of the shipping lines.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Now that COVID-19 is behind us, this trusted reputation that we have built up during the crisis is now paying some dividends.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Any other clarifications for the Senior Minister of State?
